summary: Cairo is five capitals in a row: each new dynasty built its own city next to the last, and today you walk through them in order.
look: Today's route runs roughly north to south and then west: Khan el-Khalili and al-Muizz Street inside the old Fatimid walls, then south past Bab Zuwayla to Sultan Hassan and the Citadel on its spur of the Muqattam hills, and finally Abdeen Palace in the 19th-century city. From the Citadel terrace you see most of it at once: minarets and domes over flat roofs, and on a clear day the pyramids on the western horizon.
story:
Cairo was not founded once. It was founded again and again, each new ruler building his own capital beside the old one. The Arab commander Amr ibn al-As conquered Egypt in 640 to 641 and, instead of ruling from Greek Alexandria, founded Fustat next to the Roman fortress of Babylon on the Nile. The Abbasids added al-Askar after 750. In 870 Ahmad ibn Tulun, a Turkish officer from Samarra, built al-Qata'i. The Abbasids burned it in 905 but spared his great mosque.

In 969 the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia, conquered Egypt. Their general Jawhar al-Siqilli laid out a walled palace city to the north, and when Caliph al-Mu'izz arrived in 973 it became al-Qahira, 'the Victorious', the source of the word Cairo. It was a royal enclosure closed to ordinary people: two great palaces, the mosque of al-Azhar, and a main street from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla. In 1168 the vizier Shawar set fire to Fustat so that the Crusader king Amalric could not use it.

Saladin ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and in 1176 began the Citadel on the hill to the south. The rulers moved up there and the palace city opened to merchants and common Cairenes. Under the Mamluks (1250-1517) Cairo grew into perhaps the largest city in the world outside China, with an estimated 500,000 people under al-Nasir Muhammad, and sultans lined the old main street with mosques, schools and tombs.

The Ottomans made it a provincial capital in 1517. Napoleon's army held it from 1798 to 1801, and Muhammad Ali took power in 1805. His grandson Khedive Ismail built a European-style city to the west and in 1874 moved the government to Abdeen, leaving the old city to itself, which is one reason so much survived. UNESCO listed Historic Cairo as a World Heritage site in 1979.
details: Bab al-Futuh in the north and Bab Zuwayla in the south: the Fatimid gates that bracket the 1 km of al-Muizz Street.
Bayn al-Qasrayn on al-Muizz: the open stretch where the two Fatimid palaces once faced each other.
Below the Citadel: Sultan Hassan (1363) and al-Rifa'i (finished 1912) face each other, built five centuries apart to match.
From the Citadel walls, look west: on a clear day the Giza pyramids show through the haze.
16 October 2026 is a Friday: mosques close to sightseers around the midday prayer. Spend that hour in the bazaar or a museum.
fun_fact: Cairo's name means 'the Victorious'. One old story says the city was named after the planet Mars, al-Qahir, 'the Conqueror', which was rising when the foundations were laid.
narration: You are walking through a city that was founded five times, each new ruler building his own capital next to the last. In 641 the Arab general Amr ibn al-As camped beside a Roman fortress on the Nile and founded Fustat. The Abbasids added a quarter of their own, and in 870 Ahmad ibn Tulun built another, whose great mosque still stands. In 969 the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia, conquered Egypt and walled a palace city further north. They called it al-Qahira, the Victorious, and that is where the word Cairo comes from. For two centuries it was closed to ordinary people. Then Saladin ended the Fatimid line in 1171 and began the Citadel on the hill to the south. The rulers moved up there, and the old palace city filled with merchants, schools and mosques. Under the Mamluk sultans, from 1250 to 1517, Cairo became one of the biggest cities on earth, and most of what you will see today is theirs. The Ottomans came in 1517, Napoleon in 1798, Muhammad Ali in 1805. Then Khedive Ismail built a European city to the west and left the old one alone, which is partly why so much survived. Today's walk follows that story in order: the bazaar and al-Muizz Street, then Sultan Hassan, the Citadel, and finally Ismail's Abdeen Palace. When you reach the Citadel, look west on a clear day: the pyramids sit on the horizon.

period: Fatimid 969 to the end of the Muhammad Ali dynasty, 1952
summary: Four dynasties built nearly everything you will see today. Learn who they were and you can roughly date a building by its stripes and domes.
look: Nothing single to look at: use this on the street. Striped red-and-white stone, honeycomb carving over doorways and domes of carved stone mean Mamluk. Pencil-thin minarets and big central domes mean Ottoman or Muhammad Ali. Keel-shaped arches and angular Kufic script often mean Fatimid.
story:
The Fatimids (969-1171) were Isma'ili Shia caliphs who claimed descent from Fatima, the Prophet's daughter. They came from Tunisia with an army of Kutama Berbers, founded al-Qahira and al-Azhar, and ruled a sea-to-desert empire from palaces that have vanished. Their Armenian vizier Badr al-Jamali rebuilt the walls and gates in stone between 1087 and 1092.

Saladin, a Kurdish officer sent by the Syrian ruler Nur al-Din, became vizier in 1169 and abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, turning Egypt back to Sunni Islam. His family, the Ayyubids, fought the Crusaders and began the Citadel. Their armies relied on mamluks: boys bought from the steppes, mostly Kipchak Turks, raised as Muslims, trained as cavalry and then freed.

In 1250, in the middle of Louis IX's crusade, the mamluks of the last great Ayyubid sultan seized power. In 1260 Qutuz and Baybars stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut. Historians split the Mamluk Sultanate into a Turkic 'Bahri' period (1250-1382) and a Circassian 'Burji' period (1382-1517). The throne usually passed from one ex-slave to another rather than father to son, often by murder. Yet these soldiers were the great builders of Cairo: Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad, Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay and al-Ghuri. Sultan al-Ghuri died fighting the Ottoman Selim I in 1516, and Egypt fell in 1517.

Under the Ottomans the Mamluk beys crept back to power until Napoleon arrived in 1798. Then Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer born in Kavala, in today's Greece, took over in 1805. His descendants ruled as pashas, khedives and finally kings until Farouk was overthrown in 1952.
details: Ablaq: alternating courses of dark and light stone around Mamluk doorways and windows. Spot it on the next portal you pass.
Muqarnas: honeycomb niches stepping out under a portal hood or a minaret balcony. Mamluk builders loved them.
Carved stone domes with zigzags or interlacing stars: late Mamluk, mostly 1400s and early 1500s.
Pencil-shaped minarets with conical caps: Ottoman taste. The Muhammad Ali mosque on the Citadel has two.
Keel arches and stiff, angular Kufic letters: Fatimid. See al-Azhar's courtyard and the al-Aqmar facade.
fun_fact: Mamluk means 'owned'. Barquq, once sold as a slave boy, was Egypt's strongman by 1381, when his Christian father came to Cairo, converted to Islam and took the name Anas.
narration: Here is today's cast list, so every building makes sense. First the Fatimids, Shia caliphs from Tunisia who claimed descent from Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet. They conquered Egypt in 969, founded Cairo and al-Azhar, and lived in palaces you can no longer see. Then Saladin, a Kurdish officer, who abolished their caliphate in 1171, brought Egypt back to Sunni Islam, fought the Crusaders and began the Citadel. His family, the Ayyubids, bought boys from the steppes, trained them as soldiers and freed them. These were the mamluks, a word that means owned. In 1250 the mamluks took the throne for themselves, and ten years later they beat the Mongols at Ain Jalut. For the next 267 years the crown passed from one former slave to another, often by murder, yet these men built most of what you will see today: Qalawun, Sultan Hassan, Barquq, Qaytbay and al-Ghuri. In 1517 the Ottoman Turks conquered Egypt and hanged the last Mamluk sultan at Bab Zuwayla. Finally Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer born in Kavala, in today's Greece, took power in 1805, and his family ruled until 1952. A quick key for the street: striped stone, honeycomb carving and carved stone domes are Mamluk. Pencil-thin minarets are Ottoman. Look for the stripes on the next doorway you pass.

summary: A Mamluk emir threw out the bones of the Fatimid caliphs to build a merchants' inn here, and Cairo has been shopping on their graves ever since.
look: The bazaar is a maze of lanes between al-Muizz Street on the west, al-Muski Street on the south and the al-Hussein Mosque on the east. The oldest stonework stands on Sikkat al-Badistan, the lane through the middle: Sultan al-Ghuri's two carved stone gates of 1511. The goldsmiths cluster towards al-Muizz, and the busiest souvenir lanes are near al-Hussein Square.
story:
A thousand years ago this was the southern end of the great eastern palace of the Fatimid caliphs, and the site of their mausoleum, the Turbat az-Za'faran, 'the Saffron Tomb'. When Saladin opened the royal city to everyone, merchants poured in. The old main street filled up with shops, so new trading buildings went east, towards al-Azhar and the shrine of al-Hussein.

In the 1380s, during Sultan Barquq's first reign, his Master of the Stables, Jaharkas al-Khalili, demolished the Saffron Tomb to build a big khan: an inn for travelling merchants, with storerooms round a courtyard, lodgings above and shops on the street. He reportedly tipped the bones of the Fatimid family onto the rubbish hills east of the city. His name stuck, first to the building and then to the whole district.

Around 1511 Sultan al-Ghuri pulled down al-Khalili's khan, rebuilt it and laid out a market street with monumental stone gates, perhaps copying the bedestens of rival Ottoman cities. By 1517 there were 21 khans and wikalas here; by 1798, just before Napoleon, about 39. Under the Ottomans this was the Turkish merchants' quarter. Al-Muski Street was cut through in the 19th century, and much of the eastern sector, the most touristy part, was rebuilt for Princess Shawikar in the late 1930s.

Today it sells souvenirs, antiques and jewellery, while workshops in courtyards and upper floors still beat copper and inlay boxes. Bargaining is expected and friendly. Be aware that many of the cheapest trinkets are imported; handmade brass, inlay and silver cost more and look it.
details: Bab al-Badistan and Bab al-Ghuri: al-Ghuri's carved stone gates of 1511 on Sikkat al-Badistan, the oldest structures in the bazaar.
Opposite Bab al-Ghuri: the half-ruined Wikala of Sulayman Agha al-Silahdar, built in 1837 over a Mamluk khan.
Look up and into courtyards: the workshops on upper floors make some of what is sold below. Follow the hammering.
The goldsmiths' lanes towards al-Muizz Street: this is where Cairenes buy wedding gold, sold by weight.
El Fishawi café, in an alley just off al-Hussein Square: mirrors, brass trays and mint tea since the late 1700s.
fun_fact: In the late 1400s this was Cairo's hub of foreign trade, where precious stones and slaves changed hands. The souvenir papyri came about 500 years later.
narration: You are in Khan el-Khalili, and under your feet lie the Fatimid caliphs, or rather they used to. A thousand years ago this was the end of the great eastern palace, and here stood the Saffron Tomb, where the caliphs were buried. In the 1380s an emir called Jaharkas al-Khalili, Master of the Stables to Sultan Barquq, knocked the tomb down to build a khan: an inn for travelling merchants, with storerooms round a courtyard and bedrooms above. The story goes that he threw the royal bones onto the rubbish heaps outside the walls. His name stuck to the whole district. Around 1511 Sultan al-Ghuri rebuilt the area as a grand market with stone gates, and those gates are the oldest things you can still touch here. By Napoleon's time there were about 39 khans and wikalas in this quarter. Today it is half souvenirs, half real Cairo: local families buy wedding gold from the goldsmiths, and craftsmen still hammer copper in workshops upstairs. Bargain with a smile. Start low, take your time, and be ready to walk away; nobody is offended, and a deal should leave both sides happy. Now find the lane called Sikkat al-Badistan and look for al-Ghuri's carved stone gate, Bab al-Badistan.

period: Ottoman, late 18th century (1773 or 1797; sources differ)
summary: Open round the clock, mirrors on every wall, and once the regular haunt of Naguib Mahfouz, Egypt's Nobel Prize-winning novelist.
look: A narrow alley just off al-Hussein Square, lined with small tables, brass trays and big carved wooden mirror frames on the walls. There are a few small rooms inside, but most people sit in the alley itself and watch the traffic of sellers and musicians.
story:
The café is named after its first owner, and the same family has run it for at least seven generations. Sources date its opening to 1773 or 1797; either way it is one of Egypt's oldest cafés, and it is open 24 hours a day.

In the 20th century writers and intellectuals made it their sitting room. The most famous regular was Naguib Mahfouz (1911-2006), who was born in the Gamaliya quarter a few minutes north of here and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988, still the only Egyptian to do so. His Cairo Trilogy follows one family through these streets from the First World War to 1952, and Midaq Alley is set in a lane of this quarter. The chemist Ahmed Zewail, another Egyptian Nobel laureate, was also a customer.
details: The mirrors: big carved wooden frames along the walls, the café's trademark for generations.
Order mint tea or sahlab, a hot milky drink traditionally thickened with orchid-root flour and topped with nuts and coconut.
Tissue sellers, oud players and shoe-shiners will drift past: a smile and 'la, shukran' (no, thank you) is enough.
Mahfouz's Midaq Alley is set in a lane of this same quarter, close to the Khan.
fun_fact: In 1945 Mahfouz, then a civil servant, asked to be transferred to the library in Sultan al-Ghuri's mausoleum, a short walk from here, and used the job to interview people from his childhood neighbourhood.
narration: This narrow alley of brass tables and old mirrors is El Fishawi, one of the oldest cafés in Cairo. It opened in the late 1700s, it is named after its first owner, and the same family has run it for seven generations. It never closes, day or night. In the 20th century it was a meeting place for writers, and the most famous regular was Naguib Mahfouz, who grew up in this quarter and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. His Cairo Trilogy is set in these very lanes. Order a mint tea or a hot sahlab and watch the alley go by. Then look at the walls: those big carved mirror frames are the café's trademark.

summary: Built in 972 to teach Shia Islam, al-Azhar became the most respected seat of Sunni learning in the world: a thousand-year change of heart.
look: Enter by the Barbers' Gate, Bab al-Muzayinin, then walk through a passage between two 14th-century madrasas and under the Gate of Qaytbay (1495) into the white marble courtyard. Ahead is the prayer hall, its first part Fatimid, its back half an 18th-century extension. Turn round to see the minarets of Qaytbay and al-Ghuri side by side above the way you came in. Shoes come off at the entrance; women cover hair, arms and legs (robes are usually provided), men wear long trousers.
story:
Jawhar, the general who founded Cairo, began the mosque on 4 April 970, and the first Friday prayer was held here on 22 June 972, during Ramadan. It was the congregational mosque of the new Fatimid royal city and a base for spreading Isma'ili Shia teaching. Its name, 'the resplendent', probably echoes al-Zahra, a title of Fatima, from whom the caliphs claimed descent, though another theory links it to the palaces. In 988-989 the vizier Ya'qub ibn Killis paid a group of scholars to teach here, the seed of the university.

Then the tide turned. Saladin, a Sunni, took power in 1171. His chief judge banned Friday prayers here, student stipends were cut, and the silver band naming the Fatimid caliphs was stripped from the mihrab. Nearly a century of neglect followed, until the Mamluk sultan Baybars restored the Friday sermon in 1266. Afterwards sultans competed to leave their mark: Qaytbay built a gate and minaret, al-Ghuri a two-headed minaret in 1509, while Barquq and al-Mu'ayyad both built stone minarets that were so faulty they had to be pulled down.

In the 1750s the Ottoman-era grandee Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda nearly doubled the mosque, adding a prayer hall, three gates and lodgings for students, including a hall for blind students. On 21 October 1798 a revolt against Napoleon's army started here, and the French fired on the mosque.

In 1961 the university was made a separate, state-run institution. Al-Azhar is often called the second-oldest continuously running university after al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, and its Grand Imam is the most prominent voice of Sunni Islam in Egypt. Students still come from all over the Muslim world.
details: Bab al-Muzayinin, the Barbers' Gate (1753), now the main entrance, said to be named after the barbers who shaved students' heads.
The courtyard arcades: keel-shaped arches and carved stucco panels from the Fatimid restoration of 1138.
Al-Ghuri's minaret (1509) near the entrance: it ends in two square shafts with twin bulb tops, like a pair of heads.
Beside it, Qaytbay's carved stone minaret with balconies on honeycomb muqarnas, above his gate of 1495.
In the old prayer hall, the original mihrab: the stucco carving in its semi-dome is probably Fatimid.
fun_fact: In 1800 General Kléber, commander of the French army in Egypt, was stabbed to death by an al-Azhar student, Suleiman al-Halabi. The French closed the mosque until August 1801.
narration: In front of you is al-Azhar, the first mosque of Cairo and one of the oldest universities in the world. Work began in April 970, the year after the Fatimids conquered Egypt, and the first Friday prayer was held here in June 972. The Fatimids were Shia, and they built al-Azhar to teach their faith. The name probably means the resplendent one, an echo of Fatima, the Prophet's daughter, from whom the caliphs claimed descent. Then history flipped. Saladin, a Sunni, took power in 1171, stopped Friday prayers here and cut the teachers' pay. For almost a century the mosque was neglected, until the Mamluk sultan Baybars brought it back in 1266. After that every ambitious sultan wanted his own minaret on al-Azhar, which is why the roofline is a museum of styles. Today al-Azhar is the most respected centre of Sunni learning in the world, with students from across the Muslim world. In 1798 a revolt against Napoleon's army started here, and the French fired on the building. Shoes come off at the gate. Once you are in the white marble courtyard, turn back towards the entrance and look up: the minaret with two heads, side by side like twins, was built by Sultan al-Ghuri in 1509.

summary: Cairo's best-loved shrine is said to hold the head of the Prophet's grandson Hussein, carried here in 1153 to keep it from the Crusaders.
look: The mosque stands on the square across the road from al-Azhar, with Gothic-style pointed windows, slim Ottoman-style minarets and giant mechanical umbrellas that open to shade worshippers in the plaza. On the south side, the lower part of the gate called Bab al-Akhdar is the only Fatimid survivor, with an Ayyubid minaret of 1237 above it. Non-Muslims are usually not admitted, but you can see the outside from the square.
story:
Hussein, son of Ali and Fatima and grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, was killed at Karbala in Iraq in 680. According to Fatimid tradition his head was later buried at Ascalon on the coast of Palestine, where the vizier Badr al-Jamali built a shrine after it was 'rediscovered' in 1091. As the Crusaders advanced, Caliph al-Zafir had the casket dug up and brought to Cairo. It arrived on 2 September 1153 and was buried close to the caliphs' own Saffron Tomb. The shrine was finished in 1154. Damascus and Karbala also claim the head, but for Cairenes there is no doubt.

The building was rebuilt under the Ayyubids in 1237 and burned eleven years later. What you see is mostly Khedive Ismail's reconstruction of 1874, a mix of Gothic Revival and Ottoman styles. A side room added in 1893 keeps relics believed to have belonged to the Prophet, including part of a cloak, a staff, a sword and four hairs. The mosque was restored in 1996 and renovated again in 2022.

At the mawlid, the festival of Hussein's birthday, the square fills with Sufi orders, chanting, food stalls and huge crowds from all over Egypt.
details: South side: the lower part of Bab al-Akhdar, the 'Green Gate', is the only piece left of the 1154 Fatimid shrine.
Above that gate, the Ayyubid minaret of 1237 with carved arabesque panels, the oldest minaret here.
The giant steel-and-Teflon umbrellas over the plaza fold open mechanically to shade worshippers, on the Saudi model.
The cafés along the square: a good seat to watch families arrive after Friday prayers.
fun_fact: The relic room holds a lantern-shaped case said to contain four strands of the Prophet's hair, and a Quran on deer skin attributed to Ali himself.
narration: The mosque in front of you is al-Hussein, for many Cairenes the holiest place in the city. Tradition says it holds the head of Hussein, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at Karbala in Iraq in 680. According to the Fatimid story, the head was buried at Ascalon on the coast of Palestine. When the Crusaders closed in, the caliph had it carried to Cairo, where it arrived in September 1153 and was buried beside the tombs of the caliphs themselves. Damascus and Karbala also claim the head, but here nobody doubts it. The building you see is mostly from 1874, when Khedive Ismail rebuilt it with Gothic pointed windows and Ottoman pencil minarets. On Hussein's birthday festival the square fills with Sufi chanting and huge crowds. Non-Muslims are usually not allowed inside, so enjoy it from the square. Walk round to the south side and find the old door called the Green Gate: its lower part is the last piece of the original Fatimid shrine, and the minaret above it dates from 1237.

period: Fatimid street laid out 969-970; monuments 11th to 19th centuries
summary: One kilometre between two Fatimid gates, lined with mosques, tombs, schools and fountains from nine centuries: medieval Cairo's main street.
look: The street runs about 1 km north to south inside the old walls, from Bab al-Futuh to Bab Zuwayla, and busy al-Azhar Street cuts across it near the middle. The northern half holds the grandest buildings, above all Bayn al-Qasrayn, where Qalawun, al-Nasir Muhammad and Barquq stand shoulder to shoulder on your right as you walk south. South of al-Azhar Street it turns into a crowded market street leading past al-Ghuri to Bab Zuwayla.
story:
Jawhar laid out the street in 969-970 as the spine of the new royal city. Known as the Qasaba, it ran from Bab al-Futuh in the north to Bab Zuwayla in the south and passed between the caliphs' two great palaces, across the open square of Bayn al-Qasrayn, 'between the two palaces'. Under the Fatimids ordinary people were not allowed into the city at all.

After 1171 Saladin moved the court to the Citadel, the palaces were demolished and their sites redeveloped. The Qasaba became the most prestigious address in Cairo: the route of royal processions and the city's main market. Ayyubid and Mamluk rulers lined it with madrasas, mausoleums and mosques, each funded by a waqf, a charitable trust whose shops and rents paid the staff forever. Al-Salih Ayyub's madrasa (1250), Qalawun's complex (1285), al-Nasir Muhammad's madrasa (1303) and Barquq's (1386) all stand on the old palace square. Ottoman officials and Muhammad Ali's family later added charity fountains and houses.

In the 20th century al-Azhar Street sliced the street in two. From 1997 the government restored 34 monuments along it and about 67 nearby, repaved it in its old style, lowered some tall modern buildings and added night lighting. Some find the result a little polished, but it is the easiest place in the Islamic world to walk through so much medieval architecture in one go.

Naguib Mahfouz named the first volume of his Cairo Trilogy after this stretch: Bayn al-Qasrayn, translated as Palace Walk.
details: Bayn al-Qasrayn: Qalawun (1285), al-Nasir Muhammad (1303) and Barquq (1386) side by side on your right as you walk south.
The stretch by Qalawun is still called al-Nahhasin, the coppersmiths' street: listen for hammering in the side shops.
Small kiosks with bronze grilles are sabils, charity fountains; the Katkhuda sabil at the fork is the finest.
Cross al-Azhar Street to reach al-Ghuri's two buildings facing each other, then the twin minarets on Bab Zuwayla.
Come back after dark if you can: the façades are floodlit and the street fills with Cairene families.
fun_fact: You are walking well above the Fatimid street: when Bab Zuwayla was restored, the ground had risen nearly two metres since it was built.
narration: You are on al-Muizz Street, the old main street of Fatimid Cairo, about a kilometre long from the northern gate, Bab al-Futuh, to the southern gate, Bab Zuwayla. When the Fatimids laid it out in 969, it ran between the caliphs' two great palaces, and the stretch in the middle is still called Bayn al-Qasrayn, between the two palaces. Back then ordinary Cairenes were not even allowed inside the walls. After Saladin moved the court up to the Citadel, the palaces were pulled down and this became the most prestigious address in the city. Every sultan who could afford it wanted his tomb and his school here, on the route of the great processions, with rows of shops underneath to pay for the upkeep forever. That is why you can walk past nine centuries of buildings in twenty minutes: Fatimid mosques, Mamluk tombs, Ottoman fountains and merchant houses. From 1997 the street was restored, repaved and lit at night. Naguib Mahfouz named the first novel of his Cairo Trilogy after this stretch: Palace Walk. Walking south, look out on your right for three giant facades in a row: Sultan Qalawun, his son al-Nasir Muhammad, and Sultan Barquq.

summary: Two stone gates of 1087, built for an Armenian vizier like a Byzantine fortress, with the names of Napoleon's officers still carved on the towers.
look: Bab al-Futuh, with two rounded towers, closes the north end of al-Muizz Street. A short walk east along the same wall stands Bab al-Nasr, with square towers. Between them runs a stretch of the stone wall, with the minaret of al-Hakim's mosque built into it. Step outside the gates to see them as an attacker would have.
story:
Cairo's first walls of 969 were mud brick. In 1087 the vizier Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian general who had restored order for Caliph al-Mustansir, rebuilt them in stone, starting with Bab al-Futuh, 'the Gate of Conquests', and Bab al-Nasr, 'the Gate of Victory'. Bab Zuwayla in the south followed in 1092. The chronicler al-Maqrizi says three Christian monks from Edessa, today's Urfa in south-east Turkey, designed the gates, and the stonework does look closer to northern Syrian or Byzantine fortifications than to anything Cairo had built before.

Bab al-Futuh is 22 metres high. Its arch carries carved lozenges, and the overhang between the towers rests on brackets shaped as ram's heads: the ram is the sign of Mars, the planet linked to Cairo's name. Bab al-Nasr's square towers are carved with round shields and swords, and a panel over the arch carries the Shia creed naming Ali, the Fatimid signature.

In 1798-1801 Napoleon's army held these walls. The French named each tower after an officer, and you can still read 'Tour Julien' and 'Tour Courbin' carved near the top of Bab al-Nasr. Julien was one of Bonaparte's aides-de-camp.
details: Bab al-Futuh's outer face: two stone brackets above the arch are carved as ram's heads, the sign of Mars.
Bab al-Nasr's towers: carved round shields and swords, and the French names 'Tour Julien' and 'Tour Courbin' up high.
The panel over Bab al-Nasr's arch: the Shia creed with the name Ali, a Fatimid signature in stone.
Between the gates: al-Hakim's northern minaret, wrapped in its square bastion and built into the wall in 1087.
Ask the guardian whether the wall walk between the gates is open; access changes.
fun_fact: Just outside Bab al-Nasr lies Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, the Swiss explorer who found Abu Simbel in 1813. He died in Cairo in 1817 and was buried as 'Sheikh Ibrahim'.
narration: These are the northern gates of Fatimid Cairo, rebuilt in stone in 1087 by the vizier Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian general who had restored order for the caliph. Bab al-Futuh, the Gate of Conquests, has rounded towers. A short walk east along the wall is Bab al-Nasr, the Gate of Victory, with square towers carved with shields and swords. The chronicler al-Maqrizi says three Christian monks from Edessa, in today's Turkey, designed them, and the masonry does look more like a Byzantine fortress than anything Cairo had built before. Seven centuries later Napoleon's soldiers manned these walls, named each tower after an officer, and carved the names into the stone. And just outside Bab al-Nasr lies Burckhardt, the Swiss explorer who found Abu Simbel, which you will see tomorrow. Now look at the outer face of Bab al-Futuh, just above the arch: two stone brackets are carved as ram's heads, the sign of Mars, the planet that may have given Cairo its name.

summary: Finished by the caliph remembered as 'mad', this vast mosque has been a prison, a stable, a fortress and a school before turning white marble in 1980.
look: Just inside Bab al-Futuh, on your left as you walk in, a huge courtyard of 120 by 113 metres, more than twice the size of al-Azhar, is ringed by arcades. Since 1980 nearly everything gleams in white marble and gold trim. The two minarets stand at the front corners inside massive square bastions; the northern one is built into the city wall.
story:
Caliph al-Aziz began the mosque in 990, and his son al-Hakim inaugurated it in Ramadan 1013, spending 40,000 dinars on the building. Al-Hakim (985-1021) is the 'Mad Caliph' of Western books. In 1009 he ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem; he forced Christians and Jews to wear distinguishing marks, and chroniclers say he banned mulukhiyya and ordered women to stay indoors. Some modern historians think his enemies made a monster of him. On the night of 12-13 February 1021 he rode into the Muqattam hills and never came back; only his horse and bloodstained clothes were found. The Druze, whose faith took shape around him, revere him.

In 1010 the minarets were encased in brick bastions. Nobody knows why: one theory is political, another links it to his growing puritanism. Later the mosque decayed. It held Crusader prisoners, was a stable under Saladin, a fort under Napoleon, a museum from 1890 and a boys' school in the 20th century.

In 1980 the Dawoodi Bohras, an Ismaili community from India who see the Fatimids as their imams, rebuilt it in marble. Conservationists objected, but a ruin became a working mosque again.
details: The bastions round the minarets: the original towers of 1003 survive inside; the tops were rebuilt after the 1303 earthquake.
The northern minaret meets Badr al-Jamali's wall of 1087: see it from the wall side by Bab al-Futuh.
Original Fatimid survivals: carved stucco, wooden tie-beams and Kufic inscriptions along the prayer hall arches.
Bohra pilgrims: men in white with gold-trimmed caps, women in brightly coloured two-piece robes.
fun_fact: Chroniclers say al-Hakim banned mulukhiyya, the slimy green leaf stew that is now practically Egypt's national dish. Cairenes forgave him nothing and kept cooking it.
narration: You are in the mosque of al-Hakim, the second great mosque of Fatimid Cairo, twice the size of al-Azhar. It was begun in 990 and finished in 1013 by the caliph al-Hakim, a ruler Western writers call the Mad Caliph. He ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem destroyed, and chroniclers say he banned mulukhiyya stew and ordered women to stay indoors. Some historians now think his enemies exaggerated. In February 1021 he rode out alone into the Muqattam hills at night and never returned. Only his horse and his bloodstained clothes were found, and the Druze still revere him. His mosque fell on hard times: a prison for Crusader captives, a stable, a fort for Napoleon's army, a boys' school. In 1980 the Bohras, an Ismaili community from India, rebuilt it in gleaming white marble. Now look at the front corners: the minarets are wrapped in massive square bastions, added in 1010 for reasons nobody can fully explain.

summary: The best place in Cairo to see how a rich Ottoman-era family lived: a courtyard garden, screened windows and separate worlds for men and women.
look: Down Darb al-Asfar, a lane running east off al-Muizz just north of al-Aqmar, a plain door leads through a passage that turns a corner into a courtyard garden with trees. Around it rise rooms on several levels behind turned-wood mashrabiya screens. Men were received around the courtyard on the ground floor; the women's rooms are upstairs.
story:
Abd al-Wahab al-Tablawi built the house in 1648 on Darb al-Asfar, then one of the smartest and most expensive lanes in Cairo. A later owner, Hajj Ismail Shalabi, added another wing. In 1796 Sheikh Ahmad al-Suhaymi bought it and absorbed neighbouring houses into it. His family lived here for generations, until they sold it in 1931 to the committee that looked after Cairo's monuments.

The plan is all about privacy and air. The entrance passage bends so that nobody at the street door can see into the courtyard. Downstairs, around the courtyard and in an open loggia, the master entertained his male guests. Upstairs, the women's quarters look down through mashrabiya screens of turned wood: from inside you see everything, from outside the screen looks solid, and the breeze passes through. The grand reception hall has marble floors, a fountain and painted wooden ceilings, and the house even had its own small bath.

The house was restored in 1996 with a grant from the Arab Fund, together with neighbouring houses, and is now a museum of how old Cairo lived.
details: The bent entrance passage: it turns so that no one at the street door could see into the family courtyard.
The maq'ad, an arched loggia upstairs facing the courtyard, where men sat in the breeze.
Upstairs, stand behind a mashrabiya: you see the courtyard clearly, while from below the screen looks solid.
The main reception hall: marble paving, a fountain in the lower centre, and painted wooden ceilings.
Look for the family's private bath, a luxury few Cairo houses had.
fun_fact: Mashrabiya probably comes from the Arabic for 'drinking': porous water jars were set in the screened niches to cool in the breeze.
narration: Welcome to Bayt al-Suhaymi, the house of a wealthy Cairo family, and one of the best places to imagine daily life in the old city. It was built in 1648 by Abd al-Wahab al-Tablawi, enlarged by a later owner, and bought in 1796 by Sheikh Ahmad al-Suhaymi, whose family absorbed the houses next door and lived here until 1931. Notice how you came in: the entrance passage turns a corner, so nobody at the street door could see into the courtyard. The whole house is built around privacy and shade. Downstairs the master received his male guests. Upstairs, the women's rooms look down through screens of turned wood called mashrabiya. You can see out, but nobody can see in, and the breeze passes through. Jars of water were set in the window niches to cool. Go upstairs and try it: stand behind a mashrabiya, look down into the courtyard garden, and imagine watching the guests arrive without ever being seen.

summary: Free water downstairs, a boys' school upstairs: Cairo's favourite kind of charity building, placed where the street forks so everyone sees it.
look: A small two-storey building on a triangle of land where al-Muizz splits into two lanes, so three of its sides stand free. Below, each side has a rounded bay on marble columns with a metal grille: this is the sabil, where water was handed out. Above, behind wooden screens under a painted roof, was the kuttab, the Quran school.
story:
Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda (died 1776) was a Mamluk grandee who rose to command the Janissaries, the leading Ottoman army corps in Egypt, and became the greatest builder of 18th-century Cairo. He nearly doubled al-Azhar and rebuilt the dome over Qalawun's tomb. In 1744 he set this sabil-kuttab on the triangle where the street forks, so that it closes the view for anyone walking up from Bayn al-Qasrayn.

A sabil is a charity fountain. A cistern under the floor was filled with Nile water, and an attendant passed it out through the grilles, which have openings wide enough for a cup. Giving water to the thirsty is among the most praised good deeds in Islam, and a sabil kept its founder's name on people's lips. The kuttab upstairs taught local boys, often orphans, to read and recite the Quran. Cairo builders had combined the two since Mamluk times.

The style is Mamluk two centuries after the Mamluks lost power: grey and white stone with marble inlay. Inside the sabil room are Ottoman tiles, one showing the Great Mosque of Mecca, and the entrance inscription quotes the Quran's story of the People of the Cave.
details: The metal grilles of the sabil windows: openings sized so a cup could pass through to the water.
Upstairs: the kuttab's wooden screens and painted roof, where the boys sat and recited.
Inside the sabil room, if open: Ottoman tiles, including a view of the Great Mosque of Mecca.
Over the entrance: verses about the People of the Cave, a theme Katkhuda used on his buildings.
Walk all the way round: three free façades, each with its marble columns.
fun_fact: The People of the Cave in the inscription are the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, young Christians who slept for centuries in a cave near the Greek city: a story told in both the Quran and Greek Christian tradition.
narration: This little building where the street forks is a sabil-kuttab, a charity fountain with a school on top, built in 1744 by Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda, the greatest builder of 18th-century Cairo. He commanded the Janissaries, the leading Ottoman army corps in Egypt, and he also enlarged al-Azhar. Downstairs is the sabil. Under the floor was a cistern filled with Nile water, and an attendant handed out free drinks through the grilles. Giving water to the thirsty is one of the most praised good deeds in Islam, and patrons competed to put a sabil on the busiest corners. Upstairs, behind the wooden screens, was the kuttab, a primary school where local boys, often orphans, learned to read and recite the Quran. Katkhuda chose this spot so that the building closes the view for anyone walking up from the palaces. Walk round it: three sides stand free, and in each window grille you can see openings just big enough to pass a cup through.

summary: A small Fatimid mosque of 1125 that solved an old Cairo problem: its façade follows the street while the prayer hall inside turns to Mecca.
look: Easy to miss: a grey stone façade on the east side of al-Muizz, just north of the fork with the Katkhuda fountain. The doorway sits under a niche carved like a scallop shell, with a round pierced medallion in its centre. The left half of the façade is original Fatimid carving; the right half is a 1990s copy of it.
story:
The vizier al-Ma'mun al-Bata'ihi built this neighbourhood mosque in 1125 for Caliph al-Amir, near the north-east corner of the eastern palace. He did not enjoy it long: he was arrested that same year and executed three years later. 'Al-Aqmar' is usually translated 'the moonlit', one of the light names the Fatimids gave their mosques, like al-Azhar, 'the resplendent'.

Its trick was new. A mosque must face Mecca, but the street did not, so the builders aligned the façade with the street and turned the interior, making the walls thicker on one side to absorb the difference. It was also the first mosque with its whole street front covered in carving, an idea every later builder on this street copied. The medallion over the door carries the names Muhammad and Ali, a statement of the Fatimids' Shia legitimacy.

The Mamluk emir Yalbugha al-Salimi restored the mosque in the 1390s and added the minaret, whose upper part fell in 1412. In 1993 the Dawoodi Bohras renovated it and rebuilt the southern half of the façade as a copy of the northern half.
details: The shell hood over the door, ribbed like a real scallop, with a pierced medallion naming Muhammad and Ali.
The cut-off left corner: a small muqarnas niche set at an angle so traffic could turn into the side lane.
At the far left: a carved window grille, read either as a mihrab or as the window where the caliph showed himself.
Compare the halves: the left is Fatimid original; the crisper right half is the 1990s copy.
Under the cornice: fragments of the foundation inscription naming Caliph al-Amir and his vizier.
fun_fact: The angled corner may be Cairo's oldest piece of traffic engineering: carved in 1125 so that people and loaded animals could turn into the alley without scraping the wall.
narration: This small grey facade is al-Aqmar, the Moonlit Mosque, built in 1125 by the vizier al-Mamun al-Bataihi for the Fatimid caliph. The vizier did not enjoy it for long: he was arrested that same year and executed three years later. Al-Aqmar solved a problem every builder on this street would face. A mosque must face Mecca, but the street does not. So the builders made the facade follow the street and turned the prayer hall inside, making the walls thicker on one side to absorb the difference. It is also the first mosque in Cairo with its whole street front carved with decoration. Look at the doorway: above it is a niche carved like a scallop shell, and in its centre a round pierced medallion carries the names Muhammad and Ali, a statement of the Fatimids' Shia faith. Now look at the left corner of the building. It is cut off at an angle, with a small carved niche, so that people and animals could turn into the side lane without bumping into the wall.
